text: My best friend Kunal walked into the Diwali night,
Priya on his arm, lifting her up in the camera light.
And me? I couldn't even bend to touch my nani's feet.
The only reason I held my head up on that street
was what my tailor gave me just the week before. So let me take it back to the start.
Me and Priya, six long years, never did get wed, "Let's wait till you're settled," that's all she ever said. And I believed her. Gave that girl my twenties whole,
paid her EMIs, double shifts, drove her papa, played my role.
Planned every birthday while she "needed space,"
and how'd she pay me back? With my best friend's face. Kunal. My best friend since school.
Found out through his own sister in my DMs: "Bhai, I thought you should know."
Three months later, she moved out the door.
Four months on, I wasn't missing her anymore, I missed who I thought she was.
Mostly I was in pain, the kind no sleep could fix,
thirty-six, but in the mirror I looked fifty, no tricks.
Twelve-hour days on my bike, my back locked every dawn,
my knees cracked on the stairs, every bit of me was gone.
I tried it all: physio, the gym at six a.m.,
the belts, the sprays, the balms, I bought every one of them.
Painkillers till my stomach burned, the ache came right back.
My body gave up on me the same way Priya did, just like that.
Then I'm at Iqbal chacha's for my Diwali kurta fit,
twelve years he's stitched my clothes, he knows me every bit.
Mid-measurement he says, "Stand straight." I can't. He stops.
"What's going on with you?" Right there, tears dropped.
Under his counter, he pulled out a bottle with herbs on it.
"My client who's a physiotherapist put me onto this.
Not those sprays, not the YouTube nuskhe, no, fifteen Ayurvedic herbs in warm til oil, it goes in deep and slow.
"Chacha, I'm not spending more on something that does nothing."
He looked me dead in the eyes: "If it doesn't work, your stitching's free for a year."
Twelve years, never one rupee off.
So I took it home, rubbed it in every night before bed.
A week in, I texted him, "Why is this working?" I said,
"when nothing else did?" And he wrote back: "Because it was never just your back.
Twelve hours on that bike and all that stress, your muscles stayed tight, inflamed, a mess.
Sprays sit on the skin, an hour later they're gone,
warm oil massaged in slow gets down where it's wrong. No oil fixes your whole life, that's true,
but sleeping without pain is a good start for you."
It's called EIS Ayurvedic Pain Relief Oil,
Mahanarayan, Nirgundi, Ashwagandha, in a warm til oil.
Week one, I slept straight through the night. Week two, the morning stiffness started feeling light.
Week three, the stairs stopped scaring me.
A month in, cross-legged at puja, I got up free, didn't even hold the wall.
Six weeks in, the society match, twenty overs, played it all.
Not the old me. The me I was supposed to be.
Next society function, first one on the floor, in that same Diwali kurta, standing tall once more.
Nothing extra. No belt. No painkiller.
And there's Priya. Kunal next to her.
My nani walks in, I bend, touch her feet, come up smooth.
Priya's face changed, she couldn't move.
"Wow, you look really good." "Thanks." And I kept it moving.
Kunal couldn't look me in the eye.
I wasn't checking for anybody.
Priya texted that night. Left her on read.
But the moment wasn't her looking at me, it was me in the mirror, finally seeing me.
For years it said, "he's been through it." Now it says, "he's still here." I didn't need Priya to see me. I needed to see me, clear.
It's called EIS Ayurvedic Pain Relief Oil, rub it in every night. Nine ninety-nine.
If long days and stress got you stuck inside your skin, you're not alone. Ease the pain tonight, let it begin.
Fifty percent off right now, cash on delivery, if the link below is still working, grab it before it's history.
One bottle. That's all it took for me. If Priya notices next function, that's a bonus, see,
but it's not for her anymore. It's for me.
